body: The description of this PR is very verbose and hard to follow, can you please shorten it to focus on critical things or reorganize it to be clearer?

@TokageItLab I agree that accepting breaking modifications to the structure is not an easy decision, but I also genuinely believe that what this PR does is a significantly better way to work with this system moving forward. It is possible to detect the old fields when parsing the node and to convert everything to the new structure if an old version field is found. I am not sure yet how to do it smoothly though, so it will need a bit of research, but it is definitely possible to implement. It should also be possible to keep an old project compatible with this PR by baking the old settings into individual joint configs. It would take to just replace "bone_chains" with ' "bone_chains" || "settings" ' in getters/setters. The approach where you transfer the settings from one bone to the rest is not exactly the same as what this PR does. The approach works for some cases, but it absolutely doesn't for some others. For example, there are some rigging situations where you need to fine-tune the curves while watching the object move in real time, and those situations are quite common. As a user, it is possible to implement some kind of runtime settings editor and to copy the settings to the asset once you are done experimenting with them in there, but this workflow doesn't sound like working with a well-implemented engine-level system. The workflow I implemented in this PR is standard between Unity's best bone physics plugin and UE5's best bone physics plugin.
Unity's Magica Cloth UE5's Kawaii Physics
Used in most mobile gacha games. Warudo is actively adopting Magica Cloth despite having VRM Bones because it's the golden standard for Unity. Used in E33, Stellar Blade, Persona 3 Reload and many other big titles.
In case of Magica Cloth this PR basically makes it almost 1-to-1 with it. The physics settings start right below the content of the image In case of Kawaii Physics, I don't know why they made Additional Root Bones as a separate array, my assumption is that it's exactly because of old version compatibility. It is possible to implement this PR in a similar manner, but then it would be a settings array nested inside of another settings array, which would make it extremely hard to navigate and would make the UI look really crude.
And here is how the UI with this PR looks: And in the node tree you just separate it in a few groups like this: instead of having it all being clumped together in a single inspector for no reason. Regarding bone chains of different lengths. I looked up how the system calculates joints positions on the settings curves just now, and it actually needs imrovement in a different PR. Right now it just divides the current joint index by the joints count, which makes it a disaster to work with curves if you simply adjust the length of a bone in Blender and is it also makes it really inconvinient to work with curve settings on the chains that have non-uniform bones' lengths. What it should do is to add up the bone lengths up to the current joint and to divide it by the length of the whole bone chain. The current implementation assumes individual joint configs as the main workflow, but in all projects I worked on everone was using curves for that, simply because it's just a lot more convenient. I can imagine where the individual joint configs would be beneficial, hence why I kept them in this PR, but IMO those uses are very niche compared to the curve oriented workflow. With the curve oriented workflow, supporting bone chains of different lengths becomes universal and simple to implement: we just calcualte the length of every bone chain during bone chains validation and remember the maximum length. Now, instead of dividing the length up to the current joint by the length of the current chain, we divide it by the length of the longest chain, thus making all bone chains normalized relative to the longest bone chain. I went on a tangent here, but what I am trying to say is that there are a lot of issues that will significantly affect setups made for an earlier versions of this node. So if there is any point in time where some breaking changes should be made, I think it's better to be sooner rather than later.

> As a user, it is possible to implement some kind of runtime settings editor and to copy the settings to the asset once you are done experimenting with them in there, but this workflow doesn't sound like working with a well-implemented engine-level system.

I am skeptical about this opinion. For example, Magica Cloth only requires specifying the root, and it treats all children of that root as a chain. In contrast, SpringBone allows you to specify the root and end bones individually, which leads to cases like the following:

```
bone structure:
A-B-C-D-E-F-G
```
```
chains:
A-C
E-G
```

In this case, overriding all bones is not useful.

Furthermore, you would likely want to use different settings for hair and skirts. For these cases, something like an Override Group would be necessary, but the structure would likely become too complex.

> instead of having it all being clumped together in a single inspector for no reason.

While you might be able to use two SpringBoneSimulators, considering performance costs, it is recommended to use only one SpringBoneSimulator node per skeleton. The only cases where you should add multiple instances of the same SkeletonModifier are when you want to apply influences individually or when you need to explicitly control the processing order. That is why most SkeletonModifiers have a Settings struct.

Therefore, instead, it would be better to provide something like a temporary dialog for copying or overriding. This would allow for the implementation of various features, such as selecting the chains to override (apply setting) or selecting only the root to make its children a chain. There is no need to break the compatibility of SpringBone itself.

Also, I am not sure if it is worth implementing this into the engine, but in this case, an add-on might even be more useful. This is because an add-on could implement features like defining presets for overrides as resources separate from the skeleton and allowing them to be loaded via a dialog.

Eventually, I will never approve of the implementation approach of current this PR. We certainly cannot allow projects that are already using `individual_config` to be broken (Even if I were to approve it, the product team would likely not approve a change this disruptive). If we opt for a copy-based approach, it is possible to create curves by interpreting each value in `individual_config` as curve points. There is absolutely no need to deprecate `individual_config` and implement `override`.

> With the curve oriented workflow, supporting bone chains of different lengths becomes universal and simple to implement: we just calcualte the length of every bone chain during bone chains validation and remember the maximum length. Now, instead of dividing the length up to the current joint by the length of the current chain, we divide it by the length of the longest chain, thus making all bone chains normalized relative to the longest bone chain.

The feature that allows curves to take bone length into account could potentially be implemented as an option. That is adding a `bool respect_bone_length` property when `individual_config` is disabled. Then, to avoid breaking compatibility, and because enabling this would incur a bit performance cost when `mutable_bone_axes` is enabled and bone length changed, the default value should be `false`.  This is the addition of an option that does not break compatibility.

However, as I’ve said many times, overrides must be implemented as an editor-side feature like a duplicator dialog, as I mentioned above.
